papers.title: BNIP3/NIX-mediated mitophagy versus Parkin-mediated mitophagy: mechanistic differences and functional implications.
papers.summary: This paper compares two major molecular pathways cells use to selectively remove damaged mitochondria, a process called mitophagy. One pathway relies on the protein Parkin, which tags damaged mitochondria for destruction, while the other uses BNIP3 and NIX, receptor proteins that directly bind the autophagy machinery without needing Parkin. The review likely explains how these pathways differ mechanistically and what this means for cell health, especially in contexts like neurodegeneration where mitochondrial quality control is critical.
papers.why: Understanding the distinct molecular routes of mitophagy is foundational for interpreting how neuronal and interneuron mitochondrial quality control may be disrupted or visualized in your spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics studies of brain tissue.
papers.figure: A schematic comparing the molecular signaling cascades of Parkin-dependent versus BNIP3/NIX-dependent mitophagy pathways.

papers.title: Structure-based targeting of Atg8 uncovers its essential role in autophagy-mediated detoxification.
papers.summary: This paper describes a structure-based approach to specifically target Atg8, a core protein in the autophagy machinery. The researchers used this targeting strategy to reveal that Atg8 plays an essential role in detoxification processes carried out via autophagy. The study likely clarifies mechanistic details of how autophagy proteins mediate cellular clearance of harmful substances.
papers.why: Since Atg8 is a key ortholog-family component of the core autophagy machinery relevant to mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons, understanding its structural and functional roles could inform mechanistic models applicable to neuronal autophagic clearance.
papers.figure: Figure showing the structural basis of Atg8 targeting and its effect on autophagy-mediated detoxification pathways.

papers.title: NaF induced excessive autophagy of rat hippocampal neurons and NG108-15 cells via epigenetic upregulation of miR-183-5p.
papers.summary: This study investigates how sodium fluoride (NaF) exposure triggers excessive autophagy in rat hippocampal neurons and NG108-15 neuronal cells. The researchers found that NaF epigenetically increases levels of miR-183-5p, a microRNA, which in turn drives this abnormal autophagic activity. The work links an environmental toxin to disrupted neuronal autophagy through a specific molecular pathway.
papers.why: This paper's focus on molecular regulation of excessive autophagy in neurons offers mechanistic insight relevant to understanding autophagy/mitophagy dysregulation in neuronal populations, even though it doesn't directly address interneurons, perineuronal nets, or spatial omics methods.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction and PANoptosis-related signaling in acute central nervous system injuries: mechanistic convergence and therapeutic opportunities
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to PANoptosis, a form of cell death combining pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis, in acute brain and spinal cord injuries. It discusses shared molecular pathways that link damaged mitochondria to these inflammatory death cascades. The review also highlights potential therapeutic strategies that target mitochondria or PANoptosis signaling to reduce neuronal damage after acute CNS injury.
papers.why: Since mitophagy failure can trigger mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory cell death pathways, understanding PANoptosis-related signaling provides mechanistic context for interpreting mitophagy disruption in neurons studied via spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics.

papers.title: Targeting the secretory autophagy–extracellular vesicle interface: fate decisions and translational opportunities
papers.summary: This paper discusses how cells decide between degrading cellular components through autophagy or releasing them via extracellular vesicles, focusing on the molecular crossroads where these two pathways intersect. It likely reviews the regulatory machinery that controls secretory autophagy, a process where autophagy components help package and release material outside the cell rather than degrading it internally. The paper probably highlights potential therapeutic strategies for manipulating this pathway in disease contexts.
papers.why: Understanding the secretory autophagy-extracellular vesicle interface is relevant because mitophagy and autophagy pathway dysregulation in neurons may involve alternative secretory routes that affect extracellular signaling and waste clearance near perineuronal nets.

papers.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how two related calcium channels, TRPML3 and the TRPML1/3 complex, control the release of the protein MIF (macrophage migration inhibitory factor) through a non-classical secretion pathway. It finds that these channels use a protein called TMED10 and a process known as secretory autophagy to get MIF out of cells without using the usual secretion route. The study clarifies how these two related channels have distinct roles in regulating this unconventional secretion mechanism.
papers.why: Secretory autophagy and TRPML channel biology intersect with core autophagy machinery relevant to neuronal mitophagy and autophagy pathways being studied in this PhD project, even though the paper itself focuses on non-neuronal secretion.

papers.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Pretreatment Modulates Mitochondrial Quality-Control and PINK1/PARKIN-Related Gene Expression in Acute LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation.
papers.summary: This study looks at whether pretreating animals or cells with omega-3 fatty acids changes how mitochondria are managed when the brain experiences acute inflammation triggered by LPS (a bacterial toxin that mimics infection). It focuses on genes involved in PINK1/PARKIN signaling, a key pathway that tags damaged mitochondria for removal via mitophagy. The findings suggest omega-3s can shift mitochondrial quality-control gene expression, potentially offering a protective effect against neuroinflammation-induced mitochondrial damage.
papers.why: This directly relates to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy and PINK1/PARKIN-related mitochondrial quality control in neurons under inflammatory stress, offering insight into pathway modulators that could be examined spatially in future transcriptomic/metabolomic studies.
papers.figure: Figure showing relative gene expression levels of PINK1/PARKIN and other mitophagy markers across treatment groups (control, LPS, LPS+omega-3).

papers.title: NAD+ signaling in Parkinson's disease: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives
papers.summary: This paper reviews how NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) signaling is disrupted in Parkinson's disease and how this contributes to neuronal dysfunction. NAD+ is a critical molecule for mitochondrial energy production and cellular repair pathways, and its decline is linked to increased oxidative stress and impaired cellular maintenance in dopaminergic neurons. The authors discuss therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring NAD+ levels as a potential treatment approach for Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: NAD+ decline directly impacts mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy pathways in neurons, which is central to understanding neurodegeneration mechanisms relevant to this PhD project.
